title: Outlet Not Working? Why a Dead Receptacle Happens & How to Fix It
question: why is my outlet not working
summary: A dead outlet is usually a tripped GFCI or breaker, not a major failure. Reset those first, then check for a switched outlet or a loose wire before calling an electrician.

commonCauses.cause: A GFCI outlet has tripped — and it may be a different outlet on the same circuit (often in a bathroom, kitchen, garage, basement, or outdoors) that feeds this one.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Walk to every GFCI outlet in the house (the ones with TEST and RESET buttons) and press RESET. One firm click usually brings several outlets back to life.

commonCauses.cause: The circuit breaker tripped or is in a half-tripped (middle) position.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Open the breaker panel and look for a handle that's off or sitting between ON and OFF. Push it fully OFF, then firmly back ON.

commonCauses.cause: The outlet is controlled by a wall switch (a 'switched' or 'half-hot' outlet, common in living rooms and bedrooms).
commonCauses.quickCheck: Flip nearby light switches. If a lamp plugged into the top or bottom half turns on/off with a switch, the outlet is working as designed.

commonCauses.cause: A loose or backstabbed wire behind the outlet, or a loose wire on an upstream outlet feeding it.
commonCauses.quickCheck: After killing power, pull the outlet and check that wires are tight under the screws. A scorched smell, melted plastic, or warmth at the cover is a red flag — stop and call a pro.

commonCauses.cause: The outlet itself has worn out or failed internally (loose contacts from years of plugging in heavy loads).
commonCauses.quickCheck: If plugs fall out easily or the outlet only works when you wiggle the plug, the receptacle is worn and should be replaced.

commonCauses.cause: A blown fuse (in older homes with a fuse box instead of breakers).
commonCauses.quickCheck: Look at the fuse panel for a fuse with a broken metal strip or cloudy/discolored window; replace with the same amperage — never a higher one.

fixes: Test the outlet with something you know works (a phone charger or a plug-in lamp) at both the top and bottom sockets, so you're sure the outlet is actually dead and not the device.

Press RESET on every GFCI outlet in the home — bathrooms, kitchen, garage, basement, laundry, and exterior outlets. One tripped GFCI commonly kills several downstream outlets, so check them all even if they look fine.
Go to the breaker panel and find the breaker for that room. Switch it fully OFF, then firmly back ON. A tripped breaker often rests in the middle and needs a full reset, not just a nudge.
Rule out a switched outlet: flip every wall switch in the room and watch whether the outlet powers on. Many living-room and bedroom outlets are wired to a switch by design.

If the GFCI and breaker resets and switch check do not restore power, stop. A dead receptacle may still have energized conductors or an upstream fault; have a licensed electrician open boxes, test conductors, tighten connections, or replace the device.
If everything tests fine but the outlet is still dead, the break is likely upstream (a failed wire connection in another box or the panel). That tracing work is best left to a licensed electrician.
diyVsPro: DIY is limited to testing with a known-good plug-in device, checking wall switches, pressing GFCI RESET, and resetting a breaker once. Opening the receptacle box, proving absence of voltage, tightening conductors, or replacing the receptacle is licensed-electrician work in this guide.
typicalCostUSD: DIY: $0 to reset a GFCI/breaker; $3-$25 for a replacement receptacle (standard ~$3, GFCI ~$15-$25). Pro: $120-$250 for a service call to diagnose and replace an outlet; $200-$500+ if they have to trace and repair a hidden wiring fault.
timeEstimate: 5-15 minutes for resets and basic checks; 20-40 minutes to replace an outlet.
safetyNote: A dead outlet is not proof that its conductors are de-energized. Do not remove the cover plate, pull out the receptacle, or touch wiring as part of this guide. If you smell burning, see scorching, feel heat, hear arcing, or the breaker trips again after one reset, leave it off and call a licensed electrician; call emergency services for active smoke or fire.
toolsParts: Plug-in lamp or phone charger (to test for power)
